abstract.p: Industrial robots are increasingly expected to handle variation in part geometry, contact conditions and operator activity, yet many learning-based capabilities are still demonstrated mainly in simulation or short laboratory trials. This review examines how perception, robot learning, digital twins and human–robot collaboration support adaptive manufacturing, and how far physical evidence supports the performance reported for them. A critical narrative review of 80 journal publications and one industrial robot safety standard was conducted. For each primary study, the task, control interface, validation setting and reported outcome were extracted, and results from simulation, physical trials and publisher summaries were analysed separately. The control interface strongly affected transfer: in one reaching study, nominal joint-position control succeeded in 100% of simulated trials but in only 6% of physical trials, whereas joint-velocity control succeeded in all trials in both settings. In a contact-rich maze task, a retrained policy completed all six physical trials but failed when the maze geometry changed. Reported energy savings of 74.79% and 36.06% were measured against different baselines and could not be compared directly. These findings indicate that a laboratory success rate alone does not show whether a capability is ready for production. A capability-to-evidence framework is proposed that links control interfaces, test conditions and recovery behaviour to part conformance, operator workload, interventions and resource use under a released configuration. The framework provides a basis for technology selection and commissioning tests when learned robot skills are moved from the laboratory into industrial cells.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Industrial robots repeat programmed trajectories with a consistency that has made them indispensable in welding, handling, assembly and inspection. The commissioning tests, however, cover a particular set of parts, tools and operating conditions. A part arrives in an unexpected pose, friction rises as a tool wears, a fixture introduces geometric variation, or an operator steps into the shared workspace. In each case, repeatability says little about whether the task will succeed. The robot has to notice the change, choose a response and carry it out within the limits of the cell. Integrating robots with sensing and digital manufacturing infrastructure is what makes such adaptation possible [1], [2], and recent manufacturing surveys trace the same move towards data-driven, human-centric industrial artificial intelligence [3], [4].

In this review, industrial intelligence means the capacity of a robotic production system to use observations and prior knowledge to select, execute and revise actions under explicit task, safety and resource constraints. The definition covers conventional estimation and control, optimisation, learning from demonstration and reinforcement learning. It does not tie intelligence to any particular neural network, nor to unrestricted autonomy. A well-calibrated robot running a carefully designed compliant skill can be a more dependable production solution than a more general policy whose failure modes are poorly understood. The right degree of adaptation depends on the task and on what an incorrect action would cost.

Robot learning has widened the range of behaviours that can be acquired without programming every trajectory by hand. Cao et al. [5] examined how assembly and welding systems sense operator intent and share process information with the operator. Montini et al. [6] set published accounts of collaborative applications against the experience of practitioners, and Keshvarparast et al. [7] reviewed how cobots alter the design and performance of assembly systems. Taken together, these reviews show that installing a collaborative robot is not the same as achieving intelligent collaboration. Shared floor space, coordinated timing, joint task execution and reciprocal adaptation are different arrangements, and each calls for its own sensing, planning and validation, even when the robot arm is identical.

Zafar et al. [8] reviewed digital twins in collaborative robotics within Industry 5.0, and Suryoputro et al. [9] examined how manufacturing studies assess ergonomics and safety when people work alongside cobots. Human-centred production brings objectives that robot cycle time cannot capture. An allocation that shortens the robot’s trajectory may lengthen the operator’s waiting time or hand the awkward reaches to the human partner. Likewise, a digital twin improves planning only while its state, geometry and dynamics stay adequate for the decisions it informs. For these reasons, the link between individual capabilities and production outcomes has to be spelled out.

Detailed treatments of calibration, contact-rich learning, foundation models and transfer learning are now available [10], [11], [12], [13]. These studies address different control and decision problems, so they measure performance in different ways. Pose accuracy is measured in geometric space, policy success over a task distribution, and collaboration through task completion and human performance. A review that lists these technologies without examining where they meet can hide the reasons deployments fail. An accurate perception module may feed a miscalibrated frame transformation. A policy that succeeds in the laboratory may still miss a production deadline, and a safe stop can leave behind an unacceptable recovery procedure.

We take up that integration problem here. The review asks how sensing and estimation support reliable action, how learned skills interact with conventional control, and how digital twins and human models shape commissioning and operation. It then considers what evidence is needed to move from a laboratory demonstration to sustained production. Medical and service robotics are included as sources of transferable ideas about supervision, user interaction and recovery, but manufacturing remains the domain against which those ideas are judged.

Our contribution is a framework for judging how far a robotic capability supports a manufacturing decision. It ties together the information available to the robot, the authority given to its controller, the conditions under which it was tested and the consequences for production. Throughout, we separate task completion from conforming output, transfer from adaptation after retraining, and genuine energy savings from differences in the starting baseline. Five conceptual figures and seven tables carry the framework. Of the two remaining figures, one documents how the literature was identified and the other plots the simulation-to-physical gap reported in a single published study. The framework is an analytical synthesis; it is neither a new controller nor an experimentally validated architecture.

Section 2 sets out the review design and its evidence boundaries, and Section 3 develops the system architecture used for comparison. Section 4 covers perception, manipulation learning, digital twins and human collaboration. Section 5 relates these methods to manufacturing tasks and performance measures, and Section 6 considers what can be borrowed from other robotic applications. Section 7 turns to deployment requirements and research priorities, and Section 8 concludes.

sec.title: 2.1. Scope and literature identification
sec.p: We carried out a targeted critical narrative review of industrial robot intelligence across its technical and operational interfaces. Topic-specific Crossref queries were combined with searches of publisher and research-repository records (Figure 1). The Crossref searches were restricted to journal articles and used sixteen query families: industrial robot learning, contact-rich assembly, calibration, collaborative safety, digital twins, tactile manipulation, condition monitoring, cybersecurity, simulation transfer, foundation models, bin picking, ergonomic allocation, soft grippers, energy optimisation, mobile robotics and learning from demonstration.

caption.title: Literature identification, screening and evidence use

sec.p: Topic searches were added to a set of seed publications on industrial control, robot learning and cross-domain interaction. Further searches used exact article titles and combinations such as “industrial robot calibration”, “robotic assembly reinforcement learning”, “digital twin human robot collaboration” and “vision language action robotics”. Titles, publication years, author lists and persistent identifiers were checked against publisher records. Where available, final issue metadata took precedence, and an early-online date was not used as the issue year when the two differed.

Selection was purposive rather than exhaustive. The final reference set comprises 80 journal publications and ISO 10218-2:2025. Of the 80 journal publications, 75 appeared between 2023 and 2026. Five earlier papers were retained for calibration, soft robotics, rehabilitation and industrial robot control. To be included, a source had to contribute directly to an industrial capability, a deployment constraint or a clearly argued cross-domain comparison. Market forecasts, newspaper accounts, incomplete bibliographic entries and sources with no identifiable bearing on the analysis were excluded.

sec.title: 2.2. Evidence extraction and comparison
sec.p: For the detailed comparisons of control interfaces, contact-rich recovery, tactile skill organisation and digital-twin-assisted decisions, we read full article texts or accessible author manuscripts. For a small number of additional examples, only the publisher abstract was examined. Reviews supplied taxonomies and context; primary studies supplied task-specific observations. Each numerical result was recorded together with its task, comparison baseline and evidence setting, and protocol details that were not reported were left unspecified. This keeps a metric quoted in an abstract from being treated as if its full experimental protocol had been examined.

We extracted the task, robot or prototype, observation modality, policy or controller output, comparison method, validation environment, reported outcome and tested variation. Table 1 positions this synthesis against recent reviews, and Table 2 sets out the evidence rules. Where an author manuscript was consulted, its findings are attributed to the corresponding journal article, without assuming that every presentational detail matches the typeset version.

sec.title: 2.3. Synthesis procedure and limitations
sec.p: The literature was organised around a chain of dependencies: observations support state estimates, estimates inform decisions, decisions select skills, and skills generate actions under supervisory constraints. Placing findings within this chain made it possible to see which conditions recur across methods. The diagrams and recommendations that follow express this analytical synthesis and should not be read as additional experimental findings.

No pooled effect size, publication-frequency trend or statistical ranking was calculated. Task definitions, hardware, baselines and outcome measures varied too widely for an aggregate performance score to be meaningful. Nor did we carry out independent duplicate screening or a formal risk-of-bias assessment, which is why the work is presented as a critical narrative review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis. Its main limitation is selective coverage: what was accessible, and what we judged industrially relevant, shaped which evidence received attention.

sec.title: 3.1. Physical processes and information interfaces
sec.p: Figure 2 divides an intelligent robot cell into physical execution, observation and estimation, task decisions, and offline development. The physical layer contains the manipulator or mobile platform, the end-effector, fixtures, workpieces and any human partner. Cameras, joint encoders, force–torque sensors and tactile devices each capture a different aspect of this environment, and their outputs need consistent timestamps, coordinate frames and calibration before they can feed a shared state estimate. Calibration belongs to the decision chain; it is not a one-off task to be forgotten after installation [15].

caption.title: Architecture of an intelligent robot cell, with the dashed arrow denoting release of an assessed configuration [2], [14], [15], [16]

sec.p: The estimated state has to contain the variables the task depends on. For free-space transport, object pose and obstacle occupancy may be enough; during insertion, the controller also needs to know about contact and compliance. A model that labels images accurately can still fail at manipulation if it misses the contact condition that separates alignment from jamming. Conversely, an estimator need not reconstruct every physical variable when a smaller representation supports the decision at hand. What counts as a useful representation is set by the control objective and by the conditions under which a wrong inference becomes hazardous.

The task layer turns production requirements into an executable sequence. It selects an approved skill, checks prerequisites and decides when to retry, call for assistance or stop. It also links the robot to scheduling and quality systems: if inspection rejects a part, the cell needs a defined disposition for that part and a valid starting state for the next cycle. Without this link, local autonomy can leave the cell in states that downstream equipment or operators cannot interpret. Qin et al. ’s review [14] of robot digital twins likewise places manufacturing applications within an architecture that connects robot data, models and decision functions.

sec.title: 3.2. Execution authority and supervisory separation
sec.p: We distinguish three kinds of authority. Task authority governs which operation is attempted, motion authority governs how the robot moves within that operation, and safety authority governs whether motion may continue at all. A language interface may help specify a task and a learned policy may adjust a motion command, but neither function thereby qualifies to implement a safety function. The risk assessment must cover the end-effector, workpiece and surrounding machinery as well as the robot. ISO 10218-2:2025 addresses the integration and lifecycle of industrial robot applications and cells [16].

The separation matters most when models are updated after commissioning. A retrained policy can behave differently even though the robot program keeps its name. Configuration management has to bind the task definition to the policy version, calibration, tool model and approved operating envelope, and commands that are invalid for the active configuration should be rejected before execution. Safety constraints must stay in force when perception or planning fails, and any request for human intervention must leave the system in a known state.

Different update rates impose further constraints. Image understanding and task reasoning can usually run more slowly than the motion servo. Remote computation is useful for training and historical analysis, but a lost connection must never leave the robot depending on an unavailable service to reach a safe state. A practical design states what keeps running locally, what is suspended and what must be reset when data arrive late. Latency should be measured over the whole decision path under operating load, including sensor acquisition, communication and computation.

sec.title: 3.3. Adaptation across the production lifecycle
sec.p: Offline learning, commissioning and online adaptation are related but different problems. Offline learning produces a candidate behaviour from demonstrations, simulation or historical data. Commissioning then checks it against the requirements of a particular cell, and online adaptation deals with changes during operation. Evidence gathered at one stage does not carry over automatically to the others. A simulator can speed up candidate generation without showing that the real cell is safe, and a successful commissioning trial says nothing about whether unrestricted online learning would be acceptable.

Release assessment links these stages by fixing the tool, calibration, policy version and operating envelope for which acceptance has been demonstrated, as shown by the connection between offline development and execution in Figure 2. Any later policy update changes that configuration, so an explicit decision is needed on which acceptance tests still hold. This is the architectural basis for the commissioning and monitoring questions taken up in Sections 5 and 7.

sec.title: 4. Technical capabilities and their industrial constraints
4.1. Calibration and multimodal perception
sec.p: Geometric accuracy underpins every interaction between the robot and its parts, tools and external sensors. Conventional calibration identifies the parameters that relate commanded joint configurations to measured poses, while data-driven methods also learn errors that a compact physical model struggles to express. Chen et al.’s recent survey [10] covers modelling, optimisation, datasets, metrics and applications. For deployment, the difference between repeatability and absolute accuracy remains essential: a robot can return reliably to the same displaced pose and still fail a task defined in workpiece coordinates.

How far a calibration result can be trusted depends on measurement coverage. Splitting neighbouring samples at random into training and test sets can produce a flattering estimate while another region of the workspace goes untested. Holding out task-relevant configurations, loads or operating conditions is a stronger test of transfer beyond the measured set. Measurement uncertainty also has to be kept apart from compensation error: if the reference instrument and the learned model share a systematic bias, their agreement proves nothing about geometric correctness. These points argue for workspace-aware validation instead of a single mean error.

Jiang et al. [17] studied real-time calibration using camera measurements, neural networks and dimension-reduced models, relating calibration cost and parameter identifiability to the configurations available during operation. The industrial lesson is conditional. Cutting the downtime spent on measurement helps only if the retained configurations still identify the errors that matter for the intended trajectory. A new tool, payload or thermal state moves the system outside the domain over which the learned correction was evaluated, and each such change becomes an additional validation condition.

Visual perception supports object localisation, pose estimation and grasp selection. Lu et al. [18] used point clouds to segment injection-moulded corner pieces, estimate their poses and check whether the chosen surface would seal against a suction cup. Liu et al. [19] tested a contrastive six-degree-of-freedom pose estimator for picking under changes in visual conditions. Sun et al. [20] paired synthetic data generation, local grasp detection and a global search algorithm with a colour and depth (RGB-D) camera. The suction method tests a contact requirement specific to the tool, whereas the RGB-D search proposes a candidate grasp; either way, the robot still needs a collision-free path to the chosen contact. Broader context comes from the bin-picking review by Cordeiro et al. [21], the systematic review of deep grasp synthesis by Newbury et al. [22] and AnyGrasp, which reported dense grasp perception for bin clearing with a parallel gripper [23].

For this reason, an industrial comparison has to keep perception performance apart from complete picking performance. The latter also counts failed segmentation, unreachable poses, collisions rejected by the planner, slips and placement errors. Transparent or reflective parts can produce depth data unlike anything seen in training, and occlusion can leave an object easy to classify yet hard to grasp. A complete picking record lists the tested conditions, the rejected proposals and any manual clearing of the bin. Reporting only successful grasp proposals conditions the result on an earlier stage that may itself be the hard part.

After contact, tactile sensing can detect movement at the gripper that a camera outside the cell may miss. Hu et al. [24] tracked markers in tactile images to detect slip during grasping. Combining these readings with vision requires accurate timing. A controller that acts on a tactile measurement taken during slip and a camera pose acquired before contact may apply its correction to an object that has already moved.

Zhao et al. [25] reported 92.97% average grasp-stability classification accuracy on human demonstrations involving 15 objects. That figure measures classification, and its denominator differs from that of picking or placement success. Johannsmeier et al. [26] took another route, organising tactile skills by formal process specifications and testing 28 skill models with 50 executions each on the same Franka-based setup. The two studies work at complementary levels, one detecting a contact condition and the other composing an executable skill, and neither metric can stand in for the other. What matters industrially is whether the sensed condition reaches the controller in time and whether the skill ends with a conforming part.

sec.title: 4.2. Learning contact-rich manipulation
sec.p: In contact-rich operations, the motion constraints change as surfaces meet. During insertion, polishing or disassembly, a small geometric error can generate a large force when tool, robot and environment are all stiff, so a representation that serves well on approach may not serve after contact. Elguea-Aguinaco et al. relate reinforcement-learning design to these interaction requirements [11]. For manufacturing, the useful question is which part of the contact problem is being learned: search, contact-state recognition, motion correction or compliance.

Residual learning and parameter adaptation tackle different versions of this problem. A residual action modifies a nominal command, while parameter adaptation changes how an underlying controller responds; Figure 3 sets the two side by side. Residual addition only makes sense if the nominal and corrective terms share command coordinates and units, whereas compliance adaptation acts on controller parameters. An unbounded correction can work against the nominal controller, and a poorly chosen stiffness update can amplify contact loads. Bounding the final command and bounding the controller parameters protect against different failures.

Zhang et al.’s visual–force residual assembly method [27] assigned spatial search to a visual policy and interaction to a force-based policy, which makes it more specific than a generic conventional-controller-plus-residual scheme. The variation it tested covered assembly geometry, clearance and configuration, in simulation and on physical hardware. Its contribution lies in how perceptual responsibilities are divided within the policy; the publisher record, however, gives too little detail for an independent numerical comparison with the other assembly examples discussed here.

Variable-stiffness learning offers yet another interface. Ji et al. [28] investigated compliant robotic assembly, and Zhang et al. [29] evaluated safe reinforcement learning with variable impedance control in a contact-rich maze on a Franka robot. According to the latter’s author manuscript, initial physical execution succeeded in four of five trials; after observation-noise randomisation and retraining in simulation, six of six trials succeeded. A differently shaped maze still caused task failure, although no constraint violation was reported. The trial outcomes distinguish successful contact regulation after retraining from transfer to an unfamiliar geometry.

caption.title: Two policy interfaces: (a) residual action added to a nominal command and (b) adaptation of compliance parameters [27], [29], [30]

sec.p: The policy’s action space determines which dynamics are left to the low-level controller. Joint commands, Cartesian commands and compliance parameters place different demands on estimation and timing. Aljalbout et al. [30] examined these interfaces directly, and their within-study contrast is discussed in Section 4.3. Action-space choice is a major source of variation between learning systems that otherwise share observations and optimisation methods.

Temporal representation deals with a separate source of ambiguity. Chen et al. investigated latent causal factors in assembly feedback, and Wang et al. developed phase-based assembly policies with temporal learning [31], [32]. Splitting a task into phases narrows each decision, but it makes transition detection part of the control problem: a correctly learned insertion can still be triggered too early if the end of the approach is misjudged. For this reason, the whole sequence, including transitions and unsuccessful terminations, is the proper unit of evaluation.

Table 3 is organised around these interfaces. Equal training budgets do not make two policies comparable if one outputs small Cartesian increments and the other sets forces or stiffness directly. A fair baseline keeps the same distribution of initial conditions, termination rules and retry allowance, so that changes in observation processing, controller output and training curriculum can be examined one at a time. Only then can an improvement be explained rather than attributed to an algorithm name.

sec.title: 4.3. Demonstration learning and simulation transfer
sec.p: Learning from demonstration cuts down unstructured exploration by supplying an example trajectory, task sequence or feedback relation. Li et al. [33] compared ways of recording demonstrations, learning trajectories from them and optimising the resulting motion. More recent visuomotor methods learn multimodal action distributions directly from demonstrations, with Diffusion Policy as a prominent example [38]. Human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning goes a step further, combining demonstrations with online operator corrections to reach high success rates on precise assembly and dual-arm tasks after short real-world training [39]. Industrially, the question is which aspects of a demonstration stay relevant once the part or fixture changes. Exact path replay may be enough for repetitive transport, whereas a contact relation or a stable motion pattern is more useful when the goal pose varies.

The acquisition interface limits what the robot can infer. Position-only records can miss the force adjustments that made a manual insertion work, and unnecessary operator corrections can find their way into the learned behaviour. A defensible demonstration dataset records task-relevant signals and keeps successful examples apart from recovery episodes. Transfer to a new configuration is also a different test from replaying another segment of the same demonstration, and keeping the two apart is what makes a claim of skill reusability checkable.

Simulation widens the range of conditions available for policy development, but its value depends on how accurately it captures task-sensitive variables such as friction, stiffness, backlash and delay. Randomisation helps when it reflects plausible variation in the target system; arbitrary diversity can make training harder without touching the dominant mismatch. Jaquier et al.’s distinction between transfer across robots, tasks and environments is useful here [13], because a new object, a changed controller and a new robot pose different transfer problems. Figure 4 summarises the development and release sequence.

caption.title: Skill development, acceptance and operational release [13], [40], [41], [42]

sec.p: Optical tactile simulation adds a sensor-domain mismatch on top of the mechanical one. The fast optical tactile simulator (FOTS) generates tactile observations for tactile-motor learning [43]. Any test then has to ask whether both the contact response and its sensed representation support the required corrective action, since a convincing tactile image does not guarantee an accurate force or slip response. The distinction matters whenever synthetic observations are used to learn decisions whose physical consequences depend on contact.

Aljalbout et al.’s author manuscript [30] provides a direct comparison: nominal joint-position control reached 100% simulated reaching success but only 6% on the physical robot, whereas nominal joint-velocity control reported 100% in both settings. Figure 5 plots selected averages from that study. Because the authors trained several policies and evaluated a selection of them physically, the graph should be read as a within-study illustration, not as a ranking across papers.

caption.title: Simulated and physical success rates for four nominal action spaces in (a) reaching and (b) pushing, from Table I of the author manuscript of [30]

sec.p: The contrast shows how a task that looks solved in simulation can hide an unsuitable execution interface. Changing the interface changes how tracking errors, filtering and limits act on the policy, and none of this shows up in a task-success figure obtained before transfer. The evaluation should keep the deployed controller intact and report any filtering, limiting or resetting added only on the real robot. Otherwise the physical test is assessing a different closed-loop system from the one trained in simulation.

Tiwari et al. [40] reviewed the transfer of reinforcement-learning policies from simulation to physical robots, and Aljalbout et al. [44] examined how gaps between simulated and physical systems arise and how they can be measured. Outside manufacturing, champion-level drone racing [45] and agile bipedal soccer [46] show that physical transfer becomes possible when targeted dynamics randomisation, perturbations or residual models fitted to real-world data close the dominant gap. Kolb et al. [41], in turn, found that generalisation methods for assembly remain context-dependent. Figure 5 treats development as candidate generation followed by physical assessment, with rejected candidates sent back for revision. A model revised after observing physical failures has been adapted, and its later performance should not be reported as a first transfer test.

sec.title: 4.4. Digital twins and production-level decision making
sec.p: A digital twin used for robot decisions needs a defined relationship with the physical system. A geometric model is enough for collision checking. Force or energy prediction needs a dynamic model, whereas a production-flow model can schedule work without representing contact at all. Each has its own validity domain, set by the variables and interactions its decision requires. The reviews of robot digital twins and of multi-robot manufacturing bring this wider system context into view [14], [34].

Cimino et al.’s automotive assembly case illustrates the decision scope of a twin [47]. Their discrete-event model compared 64 workflows at a selected station, with three replications for the illustrated configurations, and robot assistance reduced simulated assembly time by roughly 4.4–4.6% in the reported comparisons. This is evidence for workflow analysis with a production-derived model; it is not a measurement of line-wide throughput after deployment. Its decision variables are task allocation and operation sequence, which sets it apart from the motion-parameter optimisation discussed in Section 5.3.

State synchronisation decides how long a model stays useful online. Acquisition times and configuration versions identify which geometry, tool and robot state a prediction refers to. An outdated obstacle map can make a simulated motion look feasible after the physical scene has changed, and a production-flow model can mislead when failures or manual interventions go unrecorded. Tracking predicted against observed decision variables exposes such mismatches and gives a basis for revising the model.

Human digital twins carry these requirements over to individual behaviour and workload. Baratta et al. [48] reviewed how manufacturing twins represent workers and robots and which ergonomic and time measures they support. Chand et al. [49] investigated vision-based fatigue modelling, and You et al. [50] used a human digital twin to estimate muscle fatigue and fed the estimate into task allocation during collaborative assembly. Caiazzo et al. [51] compared electroencephalographic measurements with operators’ workload ratings across three assembly scenarios. Such estimates can inform allocation, but they are not direct measurements of an operator’s internal state. A fatigue estimate inferred from posture or physiology has to be validated for the intended activity and population, and data minimisation, operator visibility and limits on secondary use become necessary once production monitoring involves personal information.

Situation awareness links the robot’s representation to collaboration: a model helps only if relevant changes are detected and communicated in time for the task. Müller et al. [52] paired an intelligent digital twin with a mobile robot platform to improve situation awareness. Their work draws attention to what the robot knows about its surroundings and how that knowledge changes, but it does not remove the need to validate navigation or task execution in the target factory. What matters is the missing or outdated state that affects the task, which visual detail alone does not supply.

sec.title: 4.5. Human collaboration and task allocation
sec.p: Human–robot collaboration requires an explicit division of responsibilities. People may supervise a largely automated operation, alternate subtasks with a robot or manipulate a shared object, and each arrangement changes how much human pose, intention and workload estimation matter. Reviews of task allocation show that assignment depends on capability, precedence and interaction requirements [35]. Allocating by nominal execution time alone can shift awkward postures or interruptions onto the operator and overstate throughput when shared tools or workspaces cause interference.

Zeng et al. combined efficiency and fatigue in production-line allocation and scheduling, and Yin et al. addressed ergonomic risk and cost in collaborative line balancing for small and medium-sized enterprises [36], [53]. Both studies argue for evaluating operator outcomes and implementation cost alongside makespan. Their optimisation objectives are nonetheless modelling choices. A weighted fatigue score is not automatically a validated measure of injury risk, and an assignment that is optimal under assumed task durations may stop being suitable when those durations change. Sensitivity analysis is the way to connect these assumptions to variation across people and to production disruptions.

Figure 6 places the operator inside the decision and feedback structure. The operator needs to understand the current task, the robot's intended action and the available ways to intervene. After a stop, the conditions that have been checked, and those still unresolved, determine whether restarting is justified. Predictability matters because a human partner coordinates with the robot over many cycles; frequent, unexplained replanning can raise monitoring effort even when every individual robot action is collision-free.

caption.title: Task allocation and feedback in human–robot coordination [35], [36], [50]

sec.p: Safety requirements have to be established for the complete application. Li et al.’s survey [54] of safe industrial collaboration covers the roles of perception, control and interaction in protecting human partners. Suitable measures depend on hazards, tool geometry, payload and foreseeable contact, and a robot sold for collaborative use does not make every application collaborative, let alone safe. Productive collaboration requires task allocation, motion behaviour and human access to agree with an independently established safety concept.

sec.title: 4.6. Foundation models and constrained task interfaces
sec.p: Foundation models bring broad visual and language representations that can help interpret instructions, identify objects and generate task plans. Reviews of large language models (LLMs), vision–language collaboration and real-world foundation-model applications describe these roles across robot systems [55], [56], [57], and recent reviews and perspectives examine their use in intelligent manufacturing [58], [59], [60]. Their value for industrial deployment is clearest when inputs and outputs carry an explicit operational meaning. Mapping an instruction onto an approved task ties language interpretation to known tools, materials and prerequisites.

Vision–language–action models bring observation and action generation closer together. Recent surveys document their architectures and applications, and broader work on robot learning places them within the development of foundation-model-based policies [37], [61]. In manufacturing, LLM agents have been tested on task-parameter matching, tool-path design and simulated robot task planning [62], on language-guided cobot navigation for tool retrieval [63] and on low-code programming of industrial robots [64]; Fan et al. found the agents more capable on planar tasks than on three-dimensional ones. Such integration does not remove the need for verification. The training data may say little about a particular industrial fixture, tolerance or hazardous tool, and an output that is semantically sensible can still be geometrically impossible or incompatible with the production sequence. A deployed system has to be checked on both counts: whether it reads the instruction correctly and whether the resulting action is physically feasible.

A practical interface restricts the model to a controlled vocabulary of skills and checks each selected skill against the current cell state. When information is missing, clarification and refusal become measurable outcomes, and ambiguous instructions, distractor objects and unavailable tools expose them far more directly than familiar, successful commands. Firoozi et al. [12] list uncertainty, real-time execution and robot-relevant data among the open challenges, and a recent review of LLMs in smart manufacturing likewise argues for keeping humans in the loop for verification and validation [65]. These constraints favour staged integration, starting with task planning and operator assistance before broader execution authority is granted. This is a deployment recommendation, not a claim that any specific architecture has been certified.

sec.title: 5. Manufacturing applications and interpretation of performance
5.1. Handling and adaptive grasping
sec.p: Bin picking and machine tending expose how perception, end-effector design and cell organisation interact. A grasp has to be reachable, hold the object during transport and present it within the placement tolerance. When a part slips, the failure may occur after the perception module has already been scored as correct. An integrated evaluation counts the whole handling operation and records where rejected or failed attempts happen.

End-effector mechanics can take care of some of these requirements. Soft grippers accommodate shape variation and can reduce local stress on fragile objects. Rus and Tolley’s foundational review explains how soft-robot design, fabrication and control are related [66], and Yasa et al. [67] survey more recent actuation, sensing, modelling and learning-based control for soft robots. Mechanical compliance, however, creates its own estimation and control problem, because deformation becomes part of the grasp state. Chen et al. [68] reported a pneumatic gripper with embedded bending sensing and characterised its operating range. Prototype results of this kind help shortlist hardware, but an industrial acceptance test must also look at wear, contamination, pressure variation and the effects of repeated cycling.

Dexterous hands allow a wider range of contacts, at the price of more sensing and coordination. Ye et al. [69] pretrained a visual–tactile representation on human demonstrations and then trained a single policy to control a multifingered hand across several manipulation tasks. For any given task, extra dexterity pays off only if it improves the complete process enough to justify the added calibration, maintenance and control complexity. A task-specific parallel or compliant gripper may still be the better choice when the part family is narrow and orientation requirements are simple. The relevant comparison includes changeover effort and failed-part handling, not the number of motions a hand can demonstrate.

sec.title: 5.2. Assembly and contact processes
sec.p: Assembly is a demanding test because pose, contact and product quality all have to be handled together. Wang et al. [32] reported an average success rate of 92.0% in physical tests of phased planetary-gear-train assembly and a 13.9% reduction in mean contact force in their algorithm comparison. The publisher summary confirms these outcomes but does not describe the full force-comparison protocol. The figures are not estimates of factory-wide yield, nor of performance under arbitrary tolerance changes. What the study does show is that phase structure and temporal learning can support physical assembly under the reported conditions.

Here the gap between task completion and acceptable output is especially important. A part can be inserted yet scratched, deformed or incompletely seated. Conversely, a controller may stop safely before damaging a part, producing a failed attempt with a good recovery outcome. Counting both kinds of event keeps productive completion apart from protective termination. A production-relevant evaluation records completion, conformance to dimensional or functional requirements, force excursions, interventions and the disposition of every unsuccessful part, and it states whether success is counted per attempt or after an allowed number of retries.

Which capability helps in a contact process depends on where the variation comes from. If the variation is geometric, calibration and localisation are the levers. Changes in friction and compliance call for interaction sensing and control, while distinct contact stages call for state recognition and skill transitions. Adding all three mechanisms without isolating their effects hides the cause of any improvement. Ablations that swap one mechanism while holding the task conditions fixed give a clearer explanation of the result.

sec.title: 5.3. Energy-aware commissioning and trajectory selection
sec.p: A robot’s energy consumption depends on trajectory, payload, configuration, speed and idle operation. Soori et al. [70] review the opportunities for reducing it, and Jiang et al. [71] showed how a long short-term memory model relating joint motion variables to consumption can drive trajectory optimisation. The accounting boundary decides what a reported saving means. Electrical input over a full production cycle includes effects that mechanical-work estimates leave out, and including auxiliary equipment can change the comparison. Cycle time and acceptable output remain constraints on any energy objective.

Mo et al.’s commissioning study [42] reported 74.79% lower energy for pick-and-place relative to an operator-defined initial motion profile, and 36.06% lower energy for welding relative to the mean of ten randomly sampled initial positions. The first search used Bayesian optimisation; the second used a genetic algorithm and changed workpiece placement. The two percentages therefore reflect different interventions and baselines of different quality. They show task-specific optimisation potential within the reported twin-assisted framework, not the savings another installation should expect.

This baseline difference changes how the results should be read. An improvement over an initial setup measures the opportunity that setup left open; it does not show superiority over a tuned energy-aware planner. A fair algorithm comparison would keep the same feasible space and production constraints and then separate search quality from the quality of the starting configuration. For this reason, Table 4 lists the two energy cases separately.

sec.p: Trajectory methods also reveal competing objectives. Wang et al. [72] studied energy-efficient planning with parallel reinforcement learning, and Chettibi [73] developed hybrid multi-objective trajectory optimisation. These are different search formulations, and comparing them in practice requires common constraints on time, smoothness and task completion. At cell level, energy per conforming output takes failed attempts and rework into account, whereas energy per attempted movement does not. This is where energy-aware planning meets the reliability measures discussed next.

sec.title: 5.4. Condition monitoring and maintenance decisions
sec.p: Robot intelligence also covers recognising degradation before it disrupts production. Lei et al. [74] reviewed condition monitoring and fault diagnosis for industrial robots, covering sensing as well as model-based and data-driven approaches, and Bogue [75] examined maintenance strategies for industrial robots and the place of predictive techniques among them. Both concern the health of the robot itself, which is a different matter from robotic inspection of other assets. The diagnostic target may be a joint, transmission, motor, sensor or the integrated robot system.

A change in current, vibration or tracking error is not necessarily a fault, since payload, speed and trajectory alter the same signals. A diagnostic model therefore needs information on operating conditions, or evidence that its decisions hold across the intended conditions. Splitting adjacent windows from the same run at random risks leaking task-specific signatures between training and testing; independent runs, operating conditions and, where claimed, robot units are more demanding tests of transfer. The origin of the faults also needs to be documented, because synthetic anomalies, injected signals and naturally developed mechanical failures are different kinds of evidence.

The value of maintenance analytics lies in the decisions they trigger and the consequences that follow. An anomaly score can be useful without pinpointing a component fault, provided its operational role is clear. On the other hand, high classification accuracy on balanced laboratory data may translate into too many false alarms when failures are rare in production. Alarm burden, detection delay and the response to an alarm connect diagnostic performance to the maintenance workflow. Remaining-life estimates follow the same logic: the operational question is whether the prediction, with its uncertainty, supports a timely inspection or maintenance decision.

sec.title: 5.5. A common evaluation basis
sec.p: Table 5 connects component measurements to the outcomes of a full production cycle. A small pose error does not guarantee successful insertion, and successful insertion does not guarantee an undamaged, conforming part. Retries and manual resets can further change the time and labour needed to produce that part. Reporting these quantities together shows where a component that works technically is still holding production back.

sec.p: The test distribution matters as much as the metric. Which objects, tolerances, operators, shifts and disturbances were tested or held out defines the scope of the result. A system tested on one robot and one fixture supports a narrower claim than one tested after changes in payload, workpiece or calibration. Automatic and manually arranged resets also impose different operational demands: a high success rate achieved with expert resets can conceal a substantial operational burden.

A useful comparison starts by identifying the configurations that meet the application’s quality and safety requirements; productivity, energy and implementation cost can then be used to choose among them. Folding every criterion into one weighted score before this check lets a throughput gain offset an unacceptable quality result. Figure 7 places the measures in Table 5 along the progression from simulation to physical testing, cell commissioning and monitored operation.

sec.title: 6. Transferable lessons from medical and service robotics
6.1. Supervision and task-specific autonomy
sec.p: Medical robotics offers a useful warning against assigning autonomy by application label. Silvera-Tawil’s survey distinguishes several categories of healthcare robot and discusses barriers to implementation [76]. Lee et al. [77] classified surgical robots cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration by task authority: of the 49 robots identified in records covering 2015–2023, 86% fell at the robot-assistance level and 6% at conditional autonomy. These figures contradict the common assumption that surgical robots are uniformly highly autonomous.

The lesson for manufacturing is to state who makes each decision and who carries out each action. A robot may automatically hold a motion constraint while a human chooses the target, or it may choose a task sequence but wait for approval before executing it. Describing these combinations makes the allocation of authority open to inspection. Clinical outcome measures and medical regulatory clearance do not carry over to a factory; what does carry over is the discipline of naming the authority a machine exercises and the conditions under which supervision changes.

sec.title: 6.2. Physical interaction and operator adaptation
sec.p: Rehabilitation robotics ties robot behaviour to an individual’s capability and response. Oña et al. [78] examined device type, treatment approach, interaction, data handling and safety in upper-limb rehabilitation. The perspective is relevant to manufacturing assistance because a human partner's physical state is not constant. Therapeutic adaptation and industrial workload allocation nonetheless pursue different goals: a clinical protocol designed to challenge a patient’s movement means something quite different from an ergonomic rule for production work.

What transfers to industry are principles of measurement and interface design. Assistance should respond to observed needs, and explicit limits and interruption options should preserve the operator’s ability to correct the robot. Human-model estimates must be validated for the specific industrial activity. Medical privacy and ethics research also draws attention to the network of people, data and organisational decisions surrounding a robot; Vallès-Peris and Domènech’s care-based framework emphasises the context of use and stakeholder involvement [79]. In a factory, this argues for involving operators and maintenance personnel in defining monitoring purposes and intervention procedures.

sec.title: 6.3. Service interaction and recovery
sec.p: Service robots work around users whose behaviour can be hard to predict. Integrating language models has widened the range of possible interaction interfaces, although communicative competence and physical task competence remain separate matters [55]. Industrial interfaces can borrow similar mechanisms to explain a fault, request a missing item or clarify an instruction. An explanation is operationally useful when it refers to the current cell state and the actions available. A fluent but wrong explanation can lead an operator to restart a process under false assumptions.

Recovery is a more productive cross-domain theme than broad claims about customer acceptance. A factory assistant needs a defined response when it cannot find a part, loses contact or receives an ambiguous instruction, and a usable recovery interface identifies the event, preserves the relevant state and tells the operator what to do. Table 6 compares the transferable principles and their limits. Software robotic process automation is left out of the physical-robot comparison because it does not share the same contact, motion and machinery hazards; it can support administrative workflows, but those benefits say nothing about the performance of a robotic production cell.

sec.title: 7.1. Safety and cybersecurity as connected operational requirements
sec.p: A robot cell combines physical hazards with information pathways, and invalid observations can produce invalid actions even when actuators and motion code behave exactly as designed. Shaik et al.’s review [80] of sensor vulnerabilities describes how sensing limitations, faults and disturbances can interact with cyber-physical threats. Data and configuration integrity thus become part of physical reliability, and fault management comes to depend on trusted observations, available cross-checks and a defined response when sources disagree.

Cybersecurity evaluation looks at the pathways through which behaviour can be altered: task commands, calibration files, learned model weights, remote maintenance interfaces and software updates. Liu et al. [81] developed the FuzzAGG framework to generate attack graphs for industrial robotic systems and evaluated it on a production-line case. We cite it to show that a robot’s communication and software dependencies can be analysed as part of the system. A security test alone, however, cannot show that the system remains physically safe under every failure it might cause.

Two implications follow for deployment. First, losing a higher-level planning or communication service must not disable the application’s safety functions. Second, recovery means checking the executable configuration, including task code, model weights and calibration, rather than simply restoring connectivity. Event records that capture those versions and the source of each command help reconstruct what the robot was authorised to do. These recommendations are our inferences from the combined safety and cybersecurity analysis, not experimental results reported by the cited studies.

sec.title: 7.2. Evidence for generalisation and continued operation
sec.p: A generalisation claim needs a named change: an unseen object, another robot, a different fixture or a disturbance absent from training. Reviews of transfer and of assembly generalisation explain why these tests are not interchangeable [13], [41]. Held-out conditions must also be kept away from reward design, controller tuning and policy selection. If retraining or online adaptation is allowed during the test, the samples, time and interventions it consumes become part of the cost of the reported performance.

Longer operation brings failure mechanisms that short demonstrations never reveal. Sensor fouling, thermal drift, gripper wear and changes in operator practice can gradually shift the observation distribution. Commissioning conditions provide the reference against which current performance is interpreted, and rising retry frequency, altered force distributions and growing manual intervention are useful warning signs. A drift alarm only has an operational consequence if it leads to inspection, recalibration or reversion to a validated mode. Continuous learning without a release procedure can leave the deployed system hard to reproduce or investigate.

Failure records show whether degradation clusters in a particular part family, contact transition or operating period. Logging the starting state, active configuration, termination reason and recovery action makes those patterns interpretable. Where production data cannot be released, an anonymised event schema and results stratified by operating condition can still support scrutiny, adding information beyond an overall success rate without exposing confidential process data.

sec.title: 7.3. Technology selection for smaller manufacturers
sec.p: Implementation cost goes well beyond buying the robot. Fixtures, sensing, integration, safety validation, staff training, maintenance and production interruption all bear on whether an adaptive system is viable. The line-balancing study of small and medium-sized enterprises explicitly links ergonomic risk with cost [53]. A more complex robot stack is justified when it tackles a recurring production problem and can be supported by the staff available. An impressive demonstration that depends on specialist intervention may be of little use to a small production team.

A practical selection procedure starts from the source of loss. Frequent manual retouching points towards better calibration or demonstration interfaces. Product variation makes a case for flexible perception and grasping, and repeated contact failures for improved force feedback and compliant skills. Where the loss comes from waiting time or workload imbalance, changing the allocation may help more than introducing a new robot-learning model. Working in this order ties technical investment to an observable production problem and provides a baseline for measuring improvement.

Resource accounting also shapes the investment decision for smaller manufacturers. Additional sensing and computation consume energy and need maintenance, whereas fewer failed parts or shorter changeovers can offset those costs. Any such comparison needs a declared boundary that includes conforming output, rework and supporting equipment. The energy studies in Section 5.3 address part of this question, but they do not capture the full service-life cost or environmental impact of adopting an intelligent robot cell.

sec.title: 7.4. Research agenda
sec.p: Our comparison points to a gap between tests of individual capabilities and tests of the complete production decision. Table 7 turns that gap into research questions. In perception, the issue is whether an uncertainty estimate usefully changes the next action; a detector that flags difficult inputs but never influences execution adds little operational value. The relevant experiments link rejection or clarification to completed tasks, damage and intervention effort.

Manufacturing foundation models

sec.p: In manipulation learning, the evidence singles out interfaces and recovery as research variables. The action-space comparison showed that simulated success can coexist with poor transfer, and the maze experiment separated constrained interaction from completion under new geometry. Future evaluations could tease these mechanisms apart by holding the task distribution fixed while varying the action interface, and by reporting performance before and after recovery. The outcome would be an explanation of where adaptation helps and where the task representation still falls short.

Digital-twin fidelity needs an equally specific target. A workflow model can support allocation while ignoring contact dynamics, and a motion model can estimate energy while ignoring operator timing. The question is which discrepancy actually changes the decision and its outcome. Comparing decisions made with updated and with stale models would show what synchronisation is worth in practice. Multi-robot manufacturing adds shared-resource constraints [34], which makes the relationship between local predictions and system-level performance especially important.

Human-centred research needs to connect estimated operator state with observable work outcomes. A fatigue-sensitive allocation is valuable when it improves the intended workload measure without creating excessive waiting or supervision, and variation across operators and shifts is part of that test. Foundation-model interfaces raise a related requirement: ambiguous instructions and unavailable skills should produce measurable clarification, refusal and handover outcomes. Together, these questions push evaluation beyond nominal success towards the conditions under which a capability can be relied on.

sec.title: 8. Conclusions
sec.p: A simulated success rate can leave the most important commissioning question unanswered. In the reaching study reviewed here, changing the action interface made little difference in simulation but changed physical success from 6% to 100%. The contact-rich maze study exposed a different limitation: a controller that completed the familiar maze after retraining still failed on a new geometry. For a prospective user, the relevant test depends on what will change in the cell, whether it is the controller, the part or the contact conditions.

The same reasoning applies at cell level. An energy estimate depends on the motion or layout used as the baseline. In collaborative assembly, a shorter robot cycle can transfer work to the operator. An acceptance test should therefore specify the starting configuration and count conforming parts, interventions and resource use over the same observation period. Recording the tool, calibration and controller version makes that test interpretable after an update.

The framework identifies which of these comparisons a published study can support. Its practical value still needs to be tested in production cells, particularly over repeated tool changes, interruptions and restarts. The studies reviewed here offer much less evidence on those conditions than on the completion of individual laboratory tasks.
